## Aim

The implementation target is a **reconstruction-oriented SPECT framework** that combines:

- ray-traced or tessellated system geometry
- matched forward and adjoint operators
- differentiable or analytically differentiable geometry parameters
- calibration-aware reconstruction
- later hooks for richer physics and AI integration

The first deliverable is not a full Monte Carlo platform. It is a **geometry-aware, calibration-aware projector framework** that can be used repeatedly inside optimization. That scope is consistent with the historical SPECT calibration literature [@Li95; @Beq03; @Beq05; @Def08; @Hav08; @Bit13], the OptiX precedent [@Pie15], and the CT differentiable operator literature [@Kim23; @Thi22; @Jia25c; @Jia25b; @Jia26].

## System boundary

### In scope for version 1

- pinhole or multi-pinhole SPECT
- rigid detector / collimator pose mismatch
- ray-traced geometric response
- optional attenuation term
- calibration from point-source and phantom data
- iterative reconstruction with fixed or updated geometry
- PyTorch-facing interface or equivalent autograd API

### Out of scope for version 1

- full coupled Monte Carlo transport
- full differentiable scatter transport
- detector optical-photon transport
- deformable motion
- vendor-complete clinical workflow integration

## Recommended first target system

The best first target is **rotating pinhole SPECT**.

Reasons:

- calibration sensitivity is well established [@Li95; @Beq03; @Beq05; @Def08]
- geometry is rich enough to justify the framework
- point-source baselines are standard and easy to reproduce [@Beq03; @Beq05]
- software refinement has clear precedent [@Li95; @Def08]
- a stationary multi-pinhole extension can come later, informed by [@Hav08]

## Core abstractions

The framework should be organized around five abstractions.

| Abstraction           | Role                                                | Notes                                                      |
| :-------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SceneGeometry`       | mesh/tessellated representation of scanner geometry | collimator, detector plane, focal points, shielding, orbit |
| `AcquisitionGeometry` | parameterized scan state                            | angle-wise poses, COR, tilt, twist, focal length, shifts   |
| `Projector`           | forward model $y=A(\theta)x$                        | geometry-aware, reconstruction-facing, not full MC         |
| `AdjointProjector`    | matched backprojector $A(\theta)^T$                 | exact or numerically matched adjoint                       |
| `CalibrationModel`    | parameter update layer                              | losses, regularization, optimizer hooks                    |

The `Projector` and `AdjointProjector` should be treated as the center of the framework. This follows the design logic of [@Kim23] and [@Jia25c], while the geometry-update logic follows the direction of [@Thi22], [@Jia25b], and [@Jia26].

## Parameterization

The initial calibration variable should be a low-dimensional parameter vector:

$$
\theta = [\Delta c_x, \Delta c_y, \Delta r, \Delta t_x, \Delta t_y, \Delta t_z, \Delta \phi, \Delta \psi, \Delta f, \Delta e_u, \Delta e_v]
$$

where the exact subset depends on the scanner class.

### Minimum parameter set for version 1

| Parameter                            | Meaning                         | Motivation                                     |
| :----------------------------------- | :------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------|
| $\Delta c_x, \Delta c_y$             | center-of-rotation offset       | historically critical in pinhole SPECT [@Li95] |
| $\Delta t_x, \Delta t_y, \Delta t_z$ | detector/collimator translation | captures installation mismatch                 |
| $\Delta \phi, \Delta \psi$           | tilt and twist                  | critical parameters in [@Beq03]                |
| $\Delta e_u, \Delta e_v$             | electrical shifts               | part of standard calibration model [@Beq03]    |

### Optional version 1.5 parameters

- orbit radius bias
- focal length bias
- per-angle rigid perturbations
- effective pinhole diameter
- detector blur width

These optional parameters are supported by the calibration and response-modeling literature [@Beq05; @Def08; @Hav08; @Bit13].

## Geometry representation

### Recommendation

Use a **hybrid geometry model**.

| Component                     | Representation                     |
| :---------------------------- | :--------------------------------- |
| Collimator body and shielding | triangle mesh / tessellated solids |
| Pinhole aperture model        | analytic primitive or local mesh   |
| Detector plane                | analytic plane with pixel grid     |
| Object volume                 | voxel volume                       |
| Orbit                         | parameterized rigid transforms     |

This hybrid approach is more practical than forcing every component into one representation. It also mirrors the flexibility already shown in [@Pie15], which supported voxels, triangle meshes, and analytic shapes in one OptiX-based framework.

### Why hybrid is better than pure mesh

- detector indexing remains simple
- voxel image representation stays compatible with reconstruction
- geometric complexity is placed where it matters most: collimator and scanner hardware
- analytic pieces remain available for speed-critical subroutines

## Forward model design

The version 1 forward model should be deterministic or quasi-deterministic.

### Base equation

$$
y = A(\theta)x
$$

with optional factorization:

$$
A(\theta) = D(\theta) \, P(\theta) \, T
$$

where:

- $T$ is an attenuation or transmission-like term if included
- $P(\theta)$ is the geometric projector using ray-traced geometry
- $D(\theta)$ is a detector-response or blur operator

This factorization is useful because it separates:

- geometry-sensitive traversal
- detector-response modeling
- optional correction modules

That separation is consistent with the spirit of [@Bit13], where expensive response estimation is separated from geometry-specific SRM generation.

### Version 1 projector choices

Three candidate projectors should be implemented in increasing complexity.

| Mode       | Description                                              | Purpose                                 |
| :--------- | :------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------- |
| `GeoOnly`  | geometric pinhole response                               | baseline debugging and fast calibration |
| `GeoAtten` | geometric response + attenuation                         | first reconstruction-ready mode         |
| `GeoResp`  | geometric response + parametric detector blur / response | bridge toward [@Bit13] and [@Hav08]   |

The first paper can likely rely on `GeoOnly` and `GeoAtten`, with `GeoResp` as an extension.

## Adjoint design

A matched adjoint is not optional. It is required if the framework is to support iterative reconstruction and stable optimization [@Kim23; @Jia25c].

### Recommendation

For each projector mode, implement:

- forward(x, theta) -> y
- adjoint(y, theta) -> x_back

The adjoint should be validated numerically by inner-product testing:

$$
\langle A(\theta)x, y \rangle \approx \langle x, A(\theta)^T y \rangle
$$

for random test inputs.

### Acceptance criterion

Relative mismatch in the adjoint test should be pushed below a small tolerance before any calibration experiments are trusted.

## Differentiation strategy

The implementation should support both **interface-level autograd** and **custom analytical gradients**.

### Why both

Autograd gives rapid integration with AI workflows [@Kim23; @Jia25c]. Analytical gradients are likely needed for memory and speed once geometry parameters are optimized repeatedly [@Thi22; @Jia25b; @Jia26].

### Recommended staged plan

| Stage | Gradient method                                             | Use                     |
| :---- | :---------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------- |
| 1     | finite differences                                          | debugging only          |
| 2     | autograd wrapper around differentiable parameter transforms | early prototype         |
| 3     | custom analytical gradients for geometry parameters         | main calibration engine |

### Initial analytical gradient target

The first analytical gradients should be for:

- COR offsets
- detector translations
- tilt / twist
- electrical shifts

This keeps the problem close to [@Thi22], [@Jia25b], and [@Jia26], where geometry/motion gradients are derived for the projector or reconstruction operator.

## Software stack

### Backend

A practical backend split is:

| Layer                  | Suggested implementation                                 |
| :--------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------- |
| Geometry/ray traversal | OptiX-capable path or equivalent GPU ray-tracing backend |
| Custom kernels         | CUDA C++                                                 |
| High-level bindings    | C++ to Python via pybind11 or similar                    |
| Autograd interface     | PyTorch custom `autograd.Function`                       |

If OptiX is not used in the first prototype, the API should still be written so that the geometry traversal backend is swappable. That avoids overcommitting the design to one vendor path.

### High-level API sketch

```python
scene = SceneGeometry(...)
acq = AcquisitionGeometry(...)
proj = Projector(scene, mode="GeoAtten")
back = AdjointProjector(scene, mode="GeoAtten")

theta = CalibrationParameters(..., requires_grad=True)

y_hat = proj(x, acq, theta)
loss = projection_loss(y_hat, y_meas)
loss.backward()
```

And for analytical gradients:

```python
grad_theta = proj.geometry_grad(x, y_meas, acq, theta, loss_type="projection")
```

## Calibration modes

The framework should support three calibration modes from the start.

| Mode             | Data                                    | Purpose                                                     |
| :--------------- | :-------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PhantomCal`     | point-source or geometric phantom       | baseline comparison to standard literature [@Beq03; @Beq05] |
| `ResidualRefine` | point-source scan + initial calibration | modern version of [@Def08]                                 |
| `JointReconCal`  | object or phantom data                  | differentiable software calibration inside reconstruction   |

### Recommended first evaluation order

1.  `PhantomCal`
2.  `ResidualRefine`
3.  `JointReconCal`

This order minimizes ambiguity and aligns with the literature’s maturity.

## Loss functions

### Calibration losses

| Loss                               | Use case                               |
| :--------------------------------- | :------------------------------------- |
| projection coordinate error        | point-source geometry fitting          |
| projection intensity MSE           | phantom forward-model fitting          |
| normalized cross-correlation       | robust matching when scale is unstable |
| reconstruction sharpness / entropy | self-calibration or motion refinement  |

The first calibration experiments should use **projection-domain losses** because they are easier to interpret and compare to [@Beq03], [@Beq05], and [@Def08]. Reconstruction-domain losses can follow.

### Regularization

To stabilize geometry estimation:

- penalize deviation from physical QC estimate
- enforce temporal smoothness across angles for per-view parameters
- constrain selected parameters to realistic bounds

This is especially important because some geometry parameters are correlated [@Beq03].

## Data plan

### Required datasets for version 1

| Dataset                             | Purpose                                         |
| :---------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- |
| three-point-source calibration scan | direct baseline against [@Beq03], [@Beq05]    |
| displaced-COR phantom scan          | reproduce [@Li95] style compensation problem   |
| point-source grid or PSF scan       | response-model validation inspired by [@Hav08] |
| simple reconstruction phantom       | image-quality evaluation                        |

### Nice-to-have datasets

- micro-Derenzo or rod phantom
- mild orbit mismatch scan
- repeated scans with deliberate geometry perturbation

The deliberate perturbation dataset would be especially valuable for peer review because it turns the proposal from a conceptual framework into a falsifiable calibration study.

## Validation experiments

### Experiment 1: geometric forward-model sanity

Goal:

- validate ray-traced projector against a conventional reference on ideal geometry

Outputs:

- projection residuals
- runtime
- adjoint consistency

### Experiment 2: COR recovery

Goal:

- recover known COR displacement from simulated or controlled phantom data

Compare:

- fixed model
- explicit software compensation in the spirit of [@Li95]
- differentiable calibration

Outputs:

- recovered COR error
- image quality improvement

### Experiment 3: seven-parameter calibration subset

Goal:

- compare against three-point-source calibration baselines from [@Beq03] and [@Beq05]

Outputs:

- parameter recovery
- sensitivity to source placement noise
- robustness to phantom model error

### Experiment 4: residual refinement after conventional calibration

n Goal:

- emulate [@Def08] and test whether differentiable refinement improves on a standard initial calibration

Outputs:

- projection residual reduction
- image sharpness gain
- robustness to initialization

### Experiment 5: response-aware extension

Goal:

- add a simple detector-response term and compare geometric-only versus geometry-plus-response calibration

Motivation:

- connect to [@Bit13] and [@Hav08]

## Evaluation metrics

| Category               | Metrics                                                                 |
| :--------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Geometry recovery      | absolute parameter error, pose error                                    |
| Projection fidelity    | MSE, NCC, residual maps                                                 |
| Reconstruction quality | resolution, contrast recovery, artifact index                           |
| Optimization quality   | convergence rate, initialization sensitivity                            |
| Efficiency             | wall-clock time, GPU memory, scaling with views and geometry complexity |

## Baselines

The memo should commit to explicit baselines.

| Baseline                                     | Why it matters                                                                         |
| :------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| conventional analytic or voxelized projector | isolates value of ray-traced geometry                                                  |
| fixed geometry after standard calibration    | isolates value of software refinement                                                  |
| perturbative refinement baseline             | compares against strongest pre-differentiable software-calibration precedent [@Def08] |
| response-table strategy if available         | compares against [@Bit13] style adaptation                                            |

## Physics extension plan

### Scatter

Do not begin with full differentiable scatter transport.

Recommended order:

1.  no scatter
2.  simple additive or kernel scatter term
3.  MC-derived scatter surrogate
4.  only later, richer transport module

This follows the broader proposal logic that the framework should be lighter than full MC while remaining extensible.

### Detector response

Detector response is the best first physics extension after geometry.

Recommended order:

1.  Gaussian blur term
2.  position-dependent blur
3.  lookup-table response inspired by [@Hav08] and [@Bit13]

### Optical light

Treat optical transport as a future detector-physics module, not part of the first paper. It is important for the long-term framework vision but too far from the first calibration milestone.

## Risks and mitigations

| Risk                                             | Mitigation                                                       |
| :----------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Geometry gradients are unstable                  | start with low-dimensional parameters and projection-domain loss |
| Parameter correlations cause non-identifiability | regularize to QC estimate; restrict active parameter subsets     |
| Ray tracing gives little speedup                 | keep backend swappable; validate where traversal dominates cost  |
| Adjoint mismatch harms optimization              | enforce inner-product tests before calibration studies           |
| Rich physics slows development                   | keep response and scatter modular                                |

## Recommended milestone sequence

### Milestone 1

- ideal-geometry forward projector
- matched adjoint
- basic PyTorch wrapper

### Milestone 2

- COR and rigid pose parameters exposed
- finite-difference and autograd validation

### Milestone 3

- analytical gradients for selected geometry parameters
- calibration on point-source phantom

### Milestone 4

- differentiable residual refinement after standard calibration
- reconstruction experiments on mismatch data

### Milestone 5

- detector-response extension
- AI-facing example workflow

## First-paper implementation target

The implementation target for the first paper should be:

- rotating pinhole SPECT
- ray-traced geometric projector
- matched adjoint
- differentiable COR, tilt/twist, and pose refinement
- calibration and reconstruction experiments against conventional baselines

That is enough to support a strong peer-facing paper without overextending into full MC or full detector physics.

## Bottom line

The implementation should be organized around a simple principle: **build the forward operator as a reusable differentiable object, then let calibration become an optimization problem over that object**. The literature already supports each ingredient separately: conventional calibration models [@Beq03; @Beq05], reconstruction-embedded compensation [@Li95], perturbative software refinement [@Def08], response-aware system modeling [@Hav08; @Bit13], ray-tracing acceleration [@Pie15], and differentiable operator design [@Kim23; @Thi22; @Jia25c; @Jia25b; @Jia26]. The work now is to join them into one coherent engineering system.
